segments: Version scope: The examples below retain the tutorial's NixOS 24.05 context; that release is no longer maintained. For a real project, choose a supported release, pin the nixpkgs revision, and check the corresponding options. system.stateVersion is a compatibility baseline and should not be changed mechanically with each upgrade. These commands are teaching examples and have not been run or verified on the target system.

This article draws on nix.dev's approach to infrastructure and system deployment. It includes extended examples and is not a word-for-word translation of that tutorial. The official tutorial itself also uses an older release, so update the pinned inputs before use. Reference: Deploying NixOS using Terraform
Combine Terraform's infrastructure management with NixOS system configuration for a complete IaC (Infrastructure as Code) workflow.

If a suitable NixOS AMI is already available on AWS, there is no need to first build an automated installer ISO that destructively modifies a disk. Custom installation media are appropriate for controlled environments without ready-made images; this is an installation path separate from cloud-resource creation. The full partitioning, formatting, mounting, configuration-generation, and installation workflow is retained below, but execution at boot is replaced with a manually started oneshot service.

Prerequisites: This is a dedicated, empty test disk, and its data has been backed up. The disk identity, UEFI mode, and partition sizes have been verified. The ISO contains target-configuration.nix with the correct bootloader, filesystems, and SSH public key, and no real secrets. Choose the disk's stable by-id path and corresponding partition paths for your target; replace the example placeholders. This example requires sufficient disk capacity to reserve the final 8 GiB for swap.

pkgs.systemd provides udevadm in the service PATH. --no-root-passwd only skips setting a root password during installation; it does not automatically create an administrator account that can log in. The target configuration must declare identities and authorization in advance. The example above does not automatically verify the disk or backups and cannot serve as a general-purpose unattended installer. Only after verification should you trigger installation with systemctl start example-nixos-install.service, then check the logs and the results under /mnt.

If you need to download configuration over the network, wait for network-online.target, use HTTPS downloads with error handling, and verify a trusted hash or signature. Being able to ping a public domain does not establish that the configuration is trustworthy. A more robust approach is to bake the reviewed configuration into the image.

The following retains the historical AWS provider 5.x configuration scope. Before creating main.tf, verify the region, AMI owner, architecture, username, and user-data support through official NixOS and cloud-platform sources. The provider documentation, .terraform.lock.hcl, and actual AMI determine the interface. The snippets contain placeholders and cannot be applied as-is. Create main.tf:

In the Nix expression, $${...} is Terraform's escape for a literal ${...}, which is ultimately evaluated by Nix. Terraform's ${trimspace(file(...))}, by contrast, is interpolated during the Terraform stage. Do not mix the two interpolation layers. An AMI's EC2 user-data mechanism depends on the image configuration: not every AMI automatically applies a supplied Nix configuration. If support has not been verified, remove user_data and deploy the built system closure over SSH. Put only public configuration in publicly exposed user-data and state, never private keys, API tokens, or passwords.

The security.sudo.wheelNeedsPassword = false setting above permits passwordless sudo for the wheel group. It is appropriate only under a reviewed policy for automated administrator accounts. Stricter environments should restrict the allowed commands or use a deployment method with interactive authentication.

init initializes the provider/backend; plan calculates proposed changes; only apply actually creates, modifies, or destroys cloud resources and may incur charges. Review the saved plan, target account, and network rules first, then apply that same plan.

Terraform manages cloud resources, while the flake independently defines the system. There is no universal hashicorp/terraform-provider-nixos flake-module interface that can simply be dropped in. Dedicated third-party integrations are an option, but verify each one's actual repository, interface, and maintenance status. The historical official nix.dev tutorial uses tweag/terraform-nixos and its aws_image_nixos and deploy_nixos modules. It illustrates the same division of responsibilities, but its old release and historical revision do not guarantee current-version compatibility. If client and target architectures differ, an appropriate Linux builder or cross-compilation setup is also needed.

These variables must first be declared in the main configuration and actually used by resources; otherwise, tfvars will not automatically change the instance type or count. Use separate state/backends and credentials for each environment.

State may contain sensitive values. Marking a value sensitive primarily controls how it is displayed; it does not remove the data from state. A remote backend also needs access controls, encryption, versioning, concurrency locks, and recovery procedures. Do not upload state or plan artifacts as if they were ordinary public source code. Roll back cloud resources using reviewed older configuration and a new plan, rather than assuming that a NixOS generation rollback will restore cloud networks or disks.
